tutorials.title: Linear Static Analysis
tutorials.summary: Bend a simple steel cantilever and learn to read displacement, stress, and support reaction.
whatYouWillBuild: A 100 x 10 x 10 mm steel cantilever fixed at one end and pulled downward by 100 N at the other.
You will compare the deformed shape, von Mises stress, tip displacement, and fixed-end reaction.
modelSetup: Open https://tunacad.com/workspace and choose Solid.
Open Solid → Box. Select the new Box in the Browser, then set Width (X) to 100 mm, Height (Y) to 10 mm, and Depth (Z) to 10 mm in Properties.
Wait for recompute to finish. Rename the Part Cantilever if desired.
Press 2 for Face selection. Click the end face at X=0 and remember it as the fixed face; then click the opposite X=100 face and remember it as the load face. Orbit slightly if an end face is hidden.
analysisSetup: Switch to Assembly and click Simulate to open the Simulation panel.
Start the local Simulation Bridge, click Detect local Bridge, enter its one-time code, and click Pair.
Enter or browse to the Gmsh and CalculiX executables and click Test Providers. Wait for both rows to show Ready.
Open Connect AI Agent, enter the AI chat, and ask it to prepare a linear-static study for the selected cantilever.
tutorials.aiPrompt: Prepare a linear-static study for my 100 x 10 x 10 mm Cantilever Part. Use steel E 210000 MPa, Poisson 0.30, density 7850 kg/m^3, yield 355 MPa. Fix the selected X=0 face and apply [0, 0, -100] N surface force to the selected X=100 face. Use second-order tetrahedra, global size 6 mm, minimum size 1.5 mm, minimum quality 0.04. Request displacement, von Mises stress, and support reaction. Prepare only; do not approve transfer.
materialProperties: Use custom isotropic steel with Young's modulus 210000 MPa, Poisson ratio 0.30, density 7850 kg/m^3, and yield strength 355 MPa.
In Material Studio, select the Cantilever Part, open Engineering, choose Custom, enter those values, and apply the material to the Part.
restraintSteps: Press 2 and select only the X=0 end face.
In the AI request call this the fixed face and request a Fixed restraint. The prepared study summary must list one fixed FACE reference.
loadSteps: Press 2 and select only the X=100 end face.
Request a surface force of [0, 0, -100] N in analysis coordinates on that face.
meshSettings: Use 3D second-order tetrahedra with global sizes 6 mm, 4.5 mm, and 3.5 mm; minimum size one quarter of the global size and minimum quality 0.04.
Run the three sizes from coarse to fine so the final comparison is meaningful.
runSteps: Send the exact values above in Connect AI and ask it to prepare, not auto-approve, the study.
Return to Simulation. Check the study card, selected Part, material, fixed face, force vector, units, and mesh size.
Click Approve geometry transfer, review the transfer confirmation, and confirm it. Approve the same immutable request in the Bridge terminal.
The status moves through queued, meshing, solving, and normalizing. Gmsh creates the tetrahedral mesh; CalculiX then solves it. Use Refresh status / results until the job succeeds.
resultSteps: Click Refresh status / results after success to open the normalized field viewer.
Choose Displacement to see where the beam moves most, then von Mises stress to see the highly loaded region near the support.
Use Deformation scale to exaggerate the bend, Clip X to look inside, and click the contour to probe a value. Confirm the support-resultant line is close to +100 N in Z.
expectedResults: Beam-theory tip displacement is 0.1919619 mm.
The recorded 3.5 mm mesh result is 0.1908403 mm on 1618 elements.
The fixed support balances the 100 N applied force; the recorded maximum von Mises stress is 55.5959 MPa.
acceptedComparison: A fine-mesh displacement from 0.1766 to 0.2073 mm is a reasonable match to the analytical value.
The 4.5-to-3.5 mm displacement change should be no more than 4%.
Reaction magnitude should be within 0.1 N of 100 N and maximum stress should be close to 55.6 MPa for the recorded mesh.
physicalMeaning: The free end moves most because bending accumulates along the beam.
Stress is highest near the fixed face because that section carries the largest bending moment.
The support reaction has the same magnitude and opposite direction as the applied load, which is the basic equilibrium check.
warnings: TunaCAD Simulation is currently experimental/beta. These tutorials are intended for learning, testing, and helping us improve the simulation workflow.
tutorials.feedback: Try this example in TunaCAD. If your result differs significantly or something does not work as shown, please report it so we can improve the simulation tools.
reproductionSteps: Create the box, assign steel, select the two end faces, prepare the study through Connect AI, approve both transfer gates, run all three meshes, and inspect displacement, stress, and reaction in the result viewer.

tutorials.title: Multi-Part and Multi-Material Analysis
tutorials.summary: Pull a bonded steel-and-aluminum bar and follow load transfer across the material interface.
whatYouWillBuild: Two 40 x 10 x 10 mm bars placed end to end along X: steel from X=0 to 40 mm and aluminum from X=40 to 80 mm.
The adjoining faces are explicitly bonded so a 100 N pull travels through both materials.
modelSetup: Open the workspace and choose Solid → Box. Set Width 40 mm, Height 10 mm, and Depth 10 mm.
Create a second Box with the same dimensions. In Properties set its X translation to 40 mm so the two end faces meet.
Keep the boxes as two Parts/domains; do not fuse them. Rename them Steel bar and Aluminum bar.
Press 2 and identify the outer X=0 support face, both meeting X=40 interface faces, and the outer X=80 load face.
analysisSetup: Switch to Assembly, click Simulate, pair the local Bridge, and click Test Providers.
Open Connect AI Agent and request a version 2 multi-domain linear-static study with an explicit bonded-tie interaction.
tutorials.aiPrompt: Prepare a version 2 multi-domain linear-static study for my two end-to-end 40 x 10 x 10 mm Parts. Assign steel E 210000 MPa, Poisson 0.30, density 7850 kg/m^3 to the first Part and aluminum E 70000 MPa, Poisson 0.33, density 2700 kg/m^3 to the second. Fix the selected outer steel face, apply [100, 0, 0] N to the selected outer aluminum face, and bond the two selected meeting faces with adjustment none and position tolerance 0.05 mm. Use second-order tetrahedra, global size 5 mm, minimum size 1.25 mm, minimum quality 0.04. Request displacement, von Mises stress, reaction, and per-domain fields. Prepare only; do not approve transfer.
materialProperties: Steel bar: Young's modulus 210000 MPa, Poisson ratio 0.30, density 7850 kg/m^3.
Aluminum bar: Young's modulus 70000 MPa, Poisson ratio 0.33, density 2700 kg/m^3.
Select each Part in turn, open Material Studio → Engineering, create the custom values, and apply them to the correct Part.
restraintSteps: Select the steel bar outer face at X=0 and request one Fixed restraint.
Confirm the approval summary assigns the support to the steel domain only.
loadSteps: Select the aluminum bar outer face at X=80 and request a [100, 0, 0] N surface force.
Select the two coincident X=40 faces and request a bonded tie with the steel face as secondary, aluminum face as primary, adjustment none, and position tolerance 0.05 mm.
meshSettings: Use second-order tetrahedra in each domain, global size 5 mm, minimum size 1.25 mm, and minimum quality 0.04.
runSteps: Ask Connect AI to prepare the two-domain study with the exact domain, material, support, load, and bonded-interface values.
In Simulation verify the approval card lists two domains, two materials, one bonded interaction, one fixed face, and one 100 N load.
Approve geometry transfer in TunaCAD, confirm the transfer summary, then approve the request in the Bridge terminal.
Watch the status pass through both domain exports, meshing, solving, and normalization.
resultSteps: Open the result viewer and leave both domain checkboxes enabled.
Switch between Displacement and von Mises stress. Toggle one domain at a time to see ownership and compare how much each material stretches.
Check Support resultants for approximately -100 N in X.
expectedResults: The recorded bonded bar displacement is between 0.00065 and 0.00090 mm.
The support reaction is approximately [-100, 0, 0] N.
Axial stress is about 1 MPa in both 100 mm² sections; aluminum contributes about three times the extension per unit length of steel.
acceptedComparison: Maximum displacement from 0.00065 to 0.00090 mm.
X reaction within 0.1 N of -100 N.
The bonded interface remains connected and both domain result controls remain available.
physicalMeaning: The same axial force crosses the bonded interface, so both bars carry nearly the same axial stress.
Aluminum stretches more because its Young's modulus is one third of steel's.
Per-domain result controls help separate material response without losing the assembly load path.
warnings: TunaCAD Simulation is currently experimental/beta. These tutorials are intended for learning, testing, and helping us improve the simulation workflow.
tutorials.feedback: Try this example in TunaCAD. If your result differs significantly or something does not work as shown, please report it so we can improve the simulation tools.
reproductionSteps: Create two end-to-end Parts, assign steel and aluminum, select support/load/interface faces, prepare the bonded study through Connect AI, approve both gates, solve, and compare both domains.

tutorials.title: Modal and Vibration Analysis
tutorials.summary: Find the natural frequencies and animated bending shapes of a fixed steel beam.
whatYouWillBuild: A 100 x 10 x 5 mm steel beam fixed at one end.
You will calculate six natural modes, select their frequencies, and animate the normalized mode shape.
modelSetup: Open Solid → Box and set Width 100 mm, Height 10 mm, and Depth 5 mm.
Wait for recompute, press 2, and select the X=0 end face for the support.
analysisSetup: Switch to Assembly, click Simulate, pair and test the local Bridge, then open Connect AI Agent.
Request Modal analysis with six modes, a 0 to 2000 Hz search range, and consistent mass. Do not add a static load.
tutorials.aiPrompt: Prepare a modal study for my 100 x 10 x 5 mm beam. Use steel E 210000 MPa, Poisson 0.30, density 7850 kg/m^3. Fix the selected X=0 face. Request 6 modes from 0 to 2000 Hz with consistent mass and normalized mode-shape fields. Use second-order tetrahedra, global size 7 mm, minimum size 2 mm, minimum quality 0.04. Prepare only; do not approve transfer.
materialProperties: Assign steel with Young's modulus 210000 MPa, Poisson ratio 0.30, and density 7850 kg/m^3. Density is required because frequency depends on mass as well as stiffness.
Use Material Studio → Engineering on the selected beam Part.
restraintSteps: Press 2 and select only the X=0 end face.
Request a Fixed restraint and confirm it appears in the study summary.
loadSteps: There is no force or pressure in this study.
Request six modes, minimum frequency 0 Hz, maximum frequency 2000 Hz, and consistent mass formulation.
meshSettings: Use 3D second-order tetrahedra, global size 7 mm, minimum size 2 mm, and minimum quality 0.04.
runSteps: Ask Connect AI to prepare the modal study with the exact material, support, mode count, frequency range, and mesh.
Review the Simulation approval card, approve geometry transfer, confirm the summary, and approve in the Bridge terminal.
During the solve Gmsh reports meshing first; CalculiX then performs the eigenvalue extraction. Refresh until the six-mode result is ready.
resultSteps: Open the result viewer. Use Mode to switch between Mode 1 through Mode 6 and read each frequency.
Keep Animate enabled and adjust Playback Hz to slow down or speed up the motion.
Change Deformation scale to make the normalized shape easy to see. This animation shows shape, not a real vibration amplitude.
expectedResults: Beam-theory first bending frequency: 417.7583 Hz.
Recorded first calculated frequency: 420.2946 Hz.
The first mode should look like a smooth cantilever bend with zero motion at the fixed face.
acceptedComparison: A first frequency from 342.6 to 492.9 Hz is within the broad analytical tutorial range; a result near 420.3 Hz matches the recorded mesh.
The fixed model should not report a rigid-body mode.
physicalMeaning: Natural frequencies are the rates at which the beam prefers to vibrate after a disturbance.
The first bending mode is usually the easiest mode to excite because it has the lowest elastic frequency.
Higher modes contain more bends and occur at higher frequencies.
warnings: TunaCAD Simulation is currently experimental/beta. These tutorials are intended for learning, testing, and helping us improve the simulation workflow.
tutorials.feedback: Try this example in TunaCAD. If your result differs significantly or something does not work as shown, please report it so we can improve the simulation tools.
reproductionSteps: Create the beam, assign density-backed steel, select the fixed face, prepare six modes through Connect AI, approve both gates, solve, and animate the mode shapes.

tutorials.title: Frictionless and Frictional Contact
tutorials.summary: Press and slide one steel block against another, then see what friction changes.
whatYouWillBuild: Two 10 x 10 x 10 mm steel blocks touching across a flat face.
You will run the same prescribed motion first without friction and then with a coefficient of 0.2.
modelSetup: Create a 10 x 10 x 10 mm Box for the fixed foundation.
Create a second 10 x 10 x 10 mm Box and translate it 10 mm in X so one face touches the foundation. Keep both as separate Parts.
Press 2 and identify the foundation outer support face, the driven-block outer face, and the two touching faces.
analysisSetup: Switch to Assembly, click Simulate, pair and test the Bridge, then open Connect AI Agent.
Request Static contact with node-to-surface linear penalty, small sliding, and no initial adjustment.
tutorials.aiPrompt: Prepare a two-domain static-contact study for my touching 10 mm steel blocks. Use E 210000 MPa and Poisson 0.30 for both. Fix the selected foundation outer face. Use the selected moving-block contact face as Secondary and foundation contact face as Primary, node-to-surface linear penalty, small sliding, no initial adjustment, and frictionless tangential behavior. Prescribe -0.001 mm normal and 0.02 mm tangential motion on the selected driven face. Use second-order tetrahedra with global size 2.5 mm and minimum quality 0.04. Request pressure, normal gap, tangential slip, displacement, stress, and reactions. Prepare only; do not approve transfer.
materialProperties: Assign both Parts isotropic steel: Young's modulus 210000 MPa and Poisson ratio 0.30.
Use Material Studio → Engineering and apply the same custom material to each selected Part.
restraintSteps: Select the foundation outer face and request a Fixed restraint.
The driven block is controlled by prescribed translation, so do not also fix it.
loadSteps: Select the touching face on the moving block as Secondary and the matching foundation face as Primary.
Run A: frictionless contact. Prescribe -0.001 mm normal motion and 0.02 mm tangential motion on the driven face.
Run B: duplicate the study and use Coulomb penalty friction with coefficient 0.2 and stick slope 5000 MPa/mm. Keep every other value unchanged.
meshSettings: Use 3D second-order tetrahedra with global size 2.5 mm, minimum size 0.625 mm, and minimum quality 0.04.
runSteps: Prepare Run A through Connect AI, check the primary/secondary labels and displacement components, then complete both approvals.
Refresh through meshing, contact iterations, and normalization until the result succeeds.
Prepare Run B by changing only tangential behavior, friction coefficient, and stick slope. Approve and solve again.
resultSteps: For each run open the result viewer and switch among Contact pressure, Normal gap / penetration, Tangential slip, and Contact shear when available.
Compare the Contact interfaces summary and Support resultants. Frictionless contact should carry almost no tangential force; the frictional run should develop shear.
Click the contour to probe local values and use both domain checkboxes to isolate a block.
expectedResults: Frictionless tangential force is approximately -0.00220 N.
For friction coefficient 0.2, recorded force on the secondary is [1058.743, -211.678, -0.814] N.
Recorded maxima are 13.5182 MPa contact pressure, 2.70364 MPa contact shear, and 0.0186929 mm tangential slip.
acceptedComparison: Frictionless tangential force should remain negligible compared with the frictional run.
Frictional pressure from 12.84 to 14.19 MPa, shear from 2.57 to 2.84 MPa, and slip from 0.0178 to 0.0196 mm are sensible comparison bands.
Tangential action and reaction should agree within 3%.
physicalMeaning: Contact pressure shows how strongly the surfaces push on each other.
Tangential slip shows relative sliding. Friction reduces that slip by creating contact shear opposite the motion.
Primary and secondary identify the projection direction used to enforce contact; they are deliberate simulation selections.
warnings: TunaCAD Simulation is currently experimental/beta. These tutorials are intended for learning, testing, and helping us improve the simulation workflow.
tutorials.feedback: Try both contact runs in TunaCAD. If your result differs significantly or something does not work as shown, please report it so we can improve the simulation tools.
reproductionSteps: Create the touching blocks, assign steel, select support/driven/contact faces, solve frictionless contact, duplicate it with friction 0.2, and compare pressure, shear, and slip.

tutorials.title: Finite Sliding and Curved Contact
tutorials.summary: Slide a block a long distance and bring a curved surface into contact across a small initial clearance.
whatYouWillBuild: Study A moves one 10 mm block 4 mm across another, which is large enough to require finite sliding.
Study B places a radius-10 mm half-cylinder 0.05 mm above a planar foundation and uses bounded initial adjustment to establish contact.
modelSetup: Study A: create two touching 10 x 10 x 10 mm boxes as separate Parts.

Study B: create a 30 x 20 x 5 mm foundation box. Create a Cylinder with radius 10 mm, height 10 mm, and angle 180 degrees; orient its axis along the contact width and position its curved surface 0.05 mm above the foundation.
Press 2 and identify each foundation support face, driven face, and the primary planar / secondary moving contact surfaces.
analysisSetup: Switch to Assembly, click Simulate, pair and test the Bridge, then open Connect AI Agent.
For both studies request Static contact with finite sliding and finite-deformation kinematics.
tutorials.aiPrompt: Prepare a two-domain finite-sliding static-contact study for the selected moving and foundation Parts. Use steel E 210000 MPa and Poisson 0.30, frictionless node-to-surface linear penalty, finite sliding, and finite-deformation kinematics. Fix the selected foundation face and use the selected moving surface as Secondary and foundation surface as Primary. For the block study prescribe -0.001 mm normal and 4 mm tangential motion with global mesh size 2.5 mm. Prepare only; do not approve transfer.
materialProperties: Assign all Parts isotropic steel with Young's modulus 210000 MPa and Poisson ratio 0.30 through Material Studio → Engineering.
restraintSteps: Fix the outer face of each foundation.
Control the moving block or half-cylinder with the prescribed-displacement values in the study rather than adding another fixed restraint.
loadSteps: Study A: frictionless finite sliding; prescribe -0.001 mm normal motion and 4 mm tangential motion.

Study B: choose the curved half-cylinder as Secondary and the plane as Primary. Set initial adjustment to Bounded to contact with maximum adjustment 0.06 mm, then use the recorded displacement-controlled approach.
The adjustment may close the 0.05 mm analysis gap but must not edit the CAD geometry.
meshSettings: Study A: second-order tetrahedra, global size 2.5 mm.
Study B: second-order tetrahedra, global size 2.25 mm; the recorded composed mesh contains 3758 nodes and 2013 elements.
Use minimum size one quarter of global size and minimum quality 0.04.
runSteps: Prepare and solve Study A first. Verify finite sliding and the 4 mm tangential component before both approvals.
Prepare Study B separately. Check the curved/planar primary-secondary assignment, 0.05 mm clearance, and 0.06 mm adjustment limit before approval.
Contact solves may show several converged increments and cutbacks. Refresh until success; a failed job does not expose partial fields.
resultSteps: For Study A view Tangential slip and Contact pressure. Confirm the interface remains active throughout the long travel.
For Study B view Normal gap / penetration and Contact pressure. Use Clip X to see the narrow curved contact zone.
Read the interface force and driven/support resultants to check that the opposing forces balance.
expectedResults: Study A: maximum slip 3.99930 mm, maximum pressure 71.5926 MPa, and 15 converged increments.
Study B: 3758 nodes, 2013 elements, peak pressure 53458.1 MPa, maximum penetration 0.0509125 mm, and balanced 87689.33 N contact/driven resultants.
acceptedComparison: Study A slip from 3.95 to 4.05 mm and pressure from 64.4 to 78.8 MPa.
Study B initial capture must stay within the 0.06 mm bound; contact and driven resultant magnitudes should agree within 0.1%.
The very high curved-contact pressure is expected for this deliberately severe numerical example.
physicalMeaning: Finite sliding updates which surface locations oppose each other as motion proceeds.
Bounded adjustment lets the analysis close a known tiny starting clearance without moving the CAD model.
Curved contact concentrates force into a small zone, so local pressure can be far higher than in flat contact.
warnings: TunaCAD Simulation is currently experimental/beta. These tutorials are intended for learning, testing, and helping us improve the simulation workflow.
tutorials.feedback: Try these contact examples in TunaCAD. If your result differs significantly or something does not work as shown, please report it so we can improve the simulation tools.
reproductionSteps: Build and solve the finite-sliding block study, then build and solve the curved half-cylinder study with bounded adjustment; compare slip, pressure, penetration, increments, and equilibrium.

tutorials.title: Geometric Nonlinear Analysis
tutorials.summary: Bend a slender beam far enough that its changing shape affects its stiffness.
whatYouWillBuild: A 150 x 10 x 5 mm steel cantilever loaded downward by 500 N.
You will compare ordinary linear response with a finite-deformation solution and inspect the load-displacement path.
modelSetup: Open Solid → Box and set Width 150 mm, Height 10 mm, and Depth 5 mm.
Press 2 and identify the X=0 fixed face and X=150 load face.
analysisSetup: Switch to Assembly, click Simulate, pair and test the Bridge, and enter Connect AI Agent.
Request Nonlinear static with geometric nonlinearity enabled, finite-deformation/finite-strain assumptions, and two ordered load ramps.
tutorials.aiPrompt: Prepare a geometric nonlinear-static study for my 150 x 10 x 5 mm steel cantilever. Use E 210000 MPa, Poisson 0.30, density 7850 kg/m^3. Fix the selected X=0 face and apply [0, 0, -500] N to the selected X=150 face. Enable finite deformation and finite strain. Use two duration-1 ramps: scale 0 to 0.5, then 0.5 to 1. Use initial increment 0.1, minimum 0.0001, maximum 0.2, maximum 200 increments, 32 iterations, cutback factor 0.25, and 8 cutbacks. Use second-order tetrahedra, global size 7.5 mm, minimum size 1.875 mm, minimum quality 0.04. Request stress, displacement, reaction, convergence, and load-displacement history. Prepare only; do not approve transfer.
materialProperties: Assign linear-elastic steel: Young's modulus 210000 MPa, Poisson ratio 0.30, density 7850 kg/m^3.
Apply it to the beam through Material Studio → Engineering.
restraintSteps: Select the X=0 end face and request one Fixed restraint.
loadSteps: Select the X=150 end face and request [0, 0, -500] N surface force.
Step 1 ramps the force scale from 0 to 0.5. Step 2 continues from 0.5 to 1.0. Each step has duration 1.
meshSettings: Reference mesh: second-order tetrahedra, global size 7.5 mm, minimum size 1.875 mm, minimum quality 0.04.
Automatic increments: initial 0.1, minimum 0.0001, maximum 0.2, maximum 200 increments, 32 iterations, cutback factor 0.25, and 8 maximum cutbacks.
For comparison, also use 10 and 6 mm meshes and maximum-increment ceilings 0.2, 0.1, and 0.05.
runSteps: Prepare the nonlinear study through Connect AI and inspect both step amplitudes and every increment control in the approval summary.
Complete the TunaCAD and Bridge approvals. Refresh while CalculiX advances through the increments.
Run a second linear-static study with the same final 500 N load for comparison.
resultSteps: Open the nonlinear result viewer and choose Displacement, then von Mises stress.
Read the nonlinear history summary and compare final displacement with the linear run.
Use Deformation scale 1 to see the actual computed deformation; increase it only when inspecting details.
expectedResults: Recorded linear displacement: 25.53123 mm.
Recorded nonlinear displacement: 24.94863 mm, with seven converged increments in each load step.
The difference is 2.2819%, and the fixed support balances the 500 N load.
acceptedComparison: Nonlinear displacement from 23.95 to 25.95 mm is a practical comparison range for the reference mesh.
Medium-to-fine displacement change below 4% and force-displacement curve change below 1%.
Both requested steps and their converged increments must appear in order.
physicalMeaning: A linear solve assumes stiffness is based on the original shape.
The nonlinear solve updates the geometry as the beam bends, so the load follows a slightly different stiffness path.
The load-displacement history shows how the response builds instead of reporting only the final point.
warnings: TunaCAD Simulation is currently experimental/beta. These tutorials are intended for learning, testing, and helping us improve the simulation workflow.
tutorials.feedback: Try this example in TunaCAD. If your result differs significantly or something does not work as shown, please report it so we can improve the simulation tools.
reproductionSteps: Create the slender beam, assign steel, select end faces, prepare two nonlinear load steps, approve both gates, solve, then compare its path and final displacement with a linear run.

tutorials.title: Elastic-Plastic Material Analysis
tutorials.summary: Pull a steel coupon past yield and inspect permanent strain, energy, and the difference from an elastic result.
whatYouWillBuild: A 100 x 10 x 10 mm steel tensile coupon fixed at one end and pulled by 30000 N.
The material uses a three-point isotropic hardening curve so you can see yielding and accumulated equivalent plastic strain.
modelSetup: Open Solid → Box and set Width 100 mm, Height 10 mm, and Depth 10 mm.
Press 2 and identify the X=0 support face and X=100 loading face.
analysisSetup: Switch to Assembly, click Simulate, pair and test the Bridge, and open Connect AI Agent.
Request Nonlinear static with finite-deformation elastic-plastic formulation and one axial tension ramp.
tutorials.aiPrompt: Prepare an elastic-plastic nonlinear-static study for my 100 x 10 x 10 mm coupon. Use E 210000 MPa, Poisson 0.30, density 7850 kg/m^3, yield 250 MPa, and isotropic hardening points (250 MPa, 0), (300 MPa, 0.02), (340 MPa, 0.08). Fix the selected X=0 face and apply [30000, 0, 0] N to the selected X=100 face in one duration-1 ramp from scale 0 to 1. Use initial increment 0.05, minimum 0.0001, maximum 0.1, maximum 250 increments, 32 iterations, cutback factor 0.25, and 8 cutbacks. Use second-order tetrahedra, global size 5 mm, minimum size 1.25 mm, minimum quality 0.04. Request displacement, stress, reaction, PEEQ, energy density, internal energy, convergence, and load-displacement history. Prepare only; do not approve transfer.
materialProperties: Elastic data: Young's modulus 210000 MPa, Poisson ratio 0.30, density 7850 kg/m^3, yield strength 250 MPa.
Choose isotropic hardening and enter true stress / plastic strain points (250 MPa, 0), (300 MPa, 0.02), and (340 MPa, 0.08).
Apply the material to the coupon through Material Studio → Engineering and include the same curve in the Connect AI preparation request.
restraintSteps: Select the X=0 end face and request a Fixed restraint.
loadSteps: Select the X=100 end face and request [30000, 0, 0] N surface force.
Use one duration-1 step with a piecewise-linear scale from 0 at time 0 to 1 at time 1.
Request displacement, von Mises stress, reaction, equivalent plastic strain, strain-energy density, internal energy, increment convergence, and load-displacement history.
meshSettings: Second-order tetrahedra, global size 5 mm, minimum size 1.25 mm, and minimum quality 0.04.
Initial increment 0.05, minimum 0.0001, maximum 0.1, maximum 250 increments, 32 iterations, cutback factor 0.25, and 8 maximum cutbacks.
runSteps: Prepare the study through Connect AI. In the approval summary check all three plastic-curve points, the axial force, requested result fields, and increment controls.
Complete both transfer approvals. Refresh while CalculiX advances through the nonlinear increments and normalizes PEEQ and energy.
For comparison, prepare a second run with the same elastic constants but without the plastic curve.
resultSteps: Open the result viewer and switch among Displacement, von Mises stress, Equivalent plastic strain, and Energy density.
PEEQ is zero before yielding and positive where permanent deformation accumulates. Click the contour to probe it.
Read total internal energy and the support reaction in the summary, then compare final displacement with the elastic-only run.
expectedResults: Recorded mesh: 434 elements. Elastic-plastic displacement is 3.7655 mm versus 0.1421 mm for the elastic comparison.
Maximum PEEQ is 0.03863676, maximum energy density is 11.28585 MPa, and total internal energy is 104210.9 N·mm.
All 434 elements yield in this uniform coupon; support reaction is -30000.02 N.
acceptedComparison: Displacement from 3.6525 to 3.8785 mm, PEEQ from 0.03555 to 0.04173, and internal energy from 99000 to 109422 N·mm.
Reaction magnitude within 3 N of 30000 N.
PEEQ and energy fields must load completely and remain finite and nonnegative.
physicalMeaning: The elastic comparison springs back along the same stiffness line, while the plastic material accumulates permanent strain after yield.
PEEQ summarizes accumulated irreversible straining; it cannot decrease during monotonic loading.
Internal energy is the work stored and dissipated inside the coupon as it deforms.
warnings: TunaCAD Simulation is currently experimental/beta. These tutorials are intended for learning, testing, and helping us improve the simulation workflow.
tutorials.feedback: Try this example in TunaCAD. If your result differs significantly or something does not work as shown, please report it so we can improve the simulation tools.
reproductionSteps: Create the coupon, assign the exact elastic-plastic curve, select support/load faces, prepare the nonlinear study, approve both gates, solve, and compare PEEQ, energy, reaction, and displacement with the elastic run.
